extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially fantasy authors) designing magic systems
extracted.subtask_short: designing magic systems for fantasy fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing and using magic systems in fantasy stories, focused on narrative utility, reader experience, and internal design principles. Intended to help authors make magic that is fun to write, satisfying to read, and useful for storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic should be fun to write
rubrics_metrics.description: As a writer, I want a system that is fun to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems that you enjoy inventing and using in scenes; author enjoyment aids sustained, creative engagement with the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic should be fun to read
rubrics_metrics.description: As a reader, I want something that is something fun to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity, wonder, and interesting consequences so readers take pleasure in encountering the magic, not just its effects on plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic must be narratively sound
rubrics_metrics.description: As a storyteller, I want a setting element that is narratively sound
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the magic's rules and presence make sense within the story’s internal logic and support story arcs rather than undermine them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave room for mystery and discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A good magic system should offer room for mystery and discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance clearly defined mechanics with unknowns so characters and readers can explore and learn over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic should be visually appealing
rubrics_metrics.description: A good magic system should be visually appealing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create evocative imagery and tangible effects that help readers picture how the magic operates and feels in the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic should enhance the mood
rubrics_metrics.description: A good magic system should work to enhance the mood of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align magical elements with tone and atmosphere so they reinforce emotional and thematic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic must facilitate the narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A good magic system should facilitate the narrative
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use magic to propel plot, create obstacles, or reveal character, rather than as an arbitrary device that short-circuits storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic should provide a source of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: A good magic system should provide a source of conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design consequences, costs, tensions, or competing interests around magic so it generates stakes and obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the Laws as guidelines, not absolute rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Though I call them laws, they’re nothing more than simple guidelines that have worked for me. Authors can violate my theories and still have good books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these principles as tools—not mandates. Deliberate, skillful breaks of these guidelines can produce strong work when done intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Law: Reader understanding vs. magical solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanderson’s First Law of Magics: An author’s ability to solve conflict with magic is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to how well the reader understands said magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If readers lack understanding of how the magic works, using it to resolve conflicts will feel unsatisfying; ensure sufficient explanation or foreshadowing before letting magic resolve key plot points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Law: Limitations are more valuable than powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanderson’s Second Law: Limitations > Powers (also noted as Ω > |).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize costs, constraints, and trade-offs in a magic system—limits create dramatic possibilities and meaningful choices more reliably than flashy abilities alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Law: Expand existing rules before adding new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanderson’s Third Law: Expand what you already have before you add something new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and deepen existing mechanics to produce novelty and escalation rather than repeatedly introducing unrelated new powers, which can bloat the system and reduce cohesion.
